blocks.body:
A friend picks a whole number from $1$ to $16$ and you may ask yes/no questions. Four questions always suffice (halve the range each time), and no strategy can guarantee fewer, because $3$ answers distinguish only $2^3 = 8$ cases. Now suppose the friend picks $1$ half of the time and spreads the other half evenly over the rest. Then it pays to ask "is it $1$?" first, and the average number of questions drops below four. How far can it drop?

Shannon's answer, from 1948, is a single number computed from the probabilities: the entropy. It measures how uncertain a random outcome is, or equivalently how much information you gain on learning it. The same quantity sets the limit for data compression, underlies the measure of difference between distributions used in statistics and machine learning, and is, up to a constant, the entropy of thermodynamics.

blocks.title: Surprise and its average
blocks.body:
If an event has probability $p$, call $\log_2(1/p)$ its surprise. A fair coin landing heads has surprise $1$; an event of probability $1/1024$ has surprise $10$. Surprise is $0$ for a certain event, grows as the event becomes rarer, and adds up for independent events, because $\log(1/(pq)) = \log(1/p) + \log(1/q)$. Up to the choice of base, these properties force the formula $\log(1/p)$ (a functional-equation argument we do not give here).

The entropy of a random variable is its average surprise. For a coin that lands heads with probability $p$ it is
$$h(p) = p\log_2\frac1p + (1-p)\log_2\frac{1}{1-p}.$$
A few values:

- $p = 0.5$: $h = 1$ bit.
- $p = 0.75$ or $0.25$: $h \approx 0.811$.
- $p = 0.9$ or $0.1$: $h \approx 0.469$.
- $p = 0.99$: $h \approx 0.081$.

A very biased coin carries little information per toss, which is why a long record of its tosses can be compressed so well: mostly it says "heads again". The function $h$ is symmetric about $1/2$, concave, and maximal at $p = 1/2$.

blocks.title: Entropy
blocks.body:
Let $X$ take finitely or countably many values with probabilities $p(x) = P(X = x)$. Its entropy is
$$H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x) = E\left[\log_2\frac{1}{p(X)}\right],$$
with the convention $0\log 0 = 0$. With $\log_2$ the unit is the bit; with the natural logarithm it is the nat, and $1$ nat $= \log_2 e \approx 1.443$ bits.

$H(X)$ depends only on the list of probabilities, not on the values $X$ takes: relabelling outcomes does not change it.

blocks.title: Range of entropy
blocks.body:
If $X$ takes at most $n$ values, then
$$0 \le H(X) \le \log_2 n.$$
$H(X) = 0$ exactly when $X$ is constant, and $H(X) = \log_2 n$ exactly when $X$ is uniform on $n$ values.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Each term $p\log_2(1/p)$ is $\ge 0$ for $0 \le p \le 1$, and is $0$ only for $p \in \{0, 1\}$; so $H \ge 0$ with equality only when one value has probability $1$.

For the upper bound, $\log_2$ is strictly concave, so by Jensen's inequality ([[convexity]])
$$H(X) = E\left[\log_2\frac{1}{p(X)}\right] \le \log_2 E\left[\frac{1}{p(X)}\right] = \log_2\sum_{x:\,p(x) > 0} p(x)\cdot\frac{1}{p(x)} = \log_2 m,$$
where $m \le n$ is the number of values of positive probability. Equality in Jensen for a strictly concave function needs $1/p(X)$ to be constant, that is, $X$ uniform on its $m$ values, and $\log_2 m = \log_2 n$ needs $m = n$.

blocks.title: Several variables: the chain rule
blocks.body:
For a pair $(X, Y)$, the joint entropy $H(X, Y)$ is the entropy of the pair viewed as one random variable. The conditional entropy
$$H(Y \mid X) = \sum_x p(x)\,H(Y \mid X = x)$$
is the uncertainty left in $Y$ once $X$ is known, averaged over $x$. Since $p(x, y) = p(x)p(y \mid x)$, taking $-\log_2$ and averaging gives the chain rule
$$H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X):$$
learning the pair is learning $X$ and then learning $Y$ given $X$. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, $H(Y \mid X) = H(Y)$ and entropies simply add. In general they are subadditive, $H(X, Y) \le H(X) + H(Y)$, and the gap
$$I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)$$
is the mutual information, the amount $X$ tells you about $Y$. The proof that $I \ge 0$ comes from the most useful inequality in the subject.

blocks.title: Relative entropy
blocks.body:
For probability distributions $p$ and $q$ on the same countable set, the relative entropy (Kullback–Leibler divergence) of $p$ from $q$ is
$$D(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_x p(x)\log_2\frac{p(x)}{q(x)},$$
summed over $x$ with $p(x) > 0$, and set to $+\infty$ if $q(x) = 0$ for some such $x$.

It measures the cost of believing the distribution is $q$ when it is really $p$. It is not symmetric, and it is not a distance in the sense of [[metric-spaces]].

blocks.title: Gibbs' inequality
blocks.body: $D(p \,\|\, q) \ge 0$, with equality if and only if $p = q$. Consequently $I(X; Y) \ge 0$, so (for variables of finite entropy) $H(X, Y) \le H(X) + H(Y)$ and $H(Y \mid X) \le H(Y)$, with equality if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Assume $D < \infty$, and let $S$ be the set where $p > 0$. By Jensen's inequality for the concave $\log_2$, applied to the variable $q(X)/p(X)$ with $X \sim p$,
$$-D(p\,\|\,q) = \sum_{x \in S} p(x)\log_2\frac{q(x)}{p(x)} \le \log_2\sum_{x \in S} p(x)\frac{q(x)}{p(x)} = \log_2\sum_{x \in S} q(x) \le \log_2 1 = 0.$$
Equality needs $q(x)/p(x)$ constant on $S$ (strict concavity) and $\sum_S q = 1$; together these force $q = p$.

For the consequence, a short calculation with $p(x, y) = p(x)p(y \mid x)$ shows that $I(X; Y) = D\big(p_{XY} \,\|\, p_X\,p_Y\big)$, the relative entropy of the joint distribution from the product of the marginals. It is $0$ exactly when $p_{XY} = p_X p_Y$, which is independence.

blocks.title: Entropy as the limit of compression
blocks.body:
A binary code assigns each outcome $x$ a string of bits $c(x)$ of length $\ell(x)$. It is a prefix code if no codeword is the beginning of another, so a stream of codewords can be decoded on the fly. The question from the introduction is a special case: a questioning strategy is a prefix code, the codeword being the sequence of answers.

Kraft's inequality, which we state with only a sketch of the reason, says that prefix codes with lengths $\ell(x)$ exist if and only if $\sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1$. (Picture an infinite binary tree: a codeword of length $\ell$ claims a subtree carrying a $2^{-\ell}$ share of the leaves at great depth, and prefix-freeness says these subtrees are disjoint.) Combining this with Gibbs' inequality gives the source coding theorem.

blocks.title: Source coding theorem
blocks.body: For any prefix code for $X$, the expected length satisfies $E[\ell(X)] \ge H(X)$. Conversely, there is a prefix code with $E[\ell(X)] < H(X) + 1$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $K = \sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1$ and define the distribution $q(x) = 2^{-\ell(x)}/K$. Then
$$E[\ell(X)] - H(X) = \sum_x p(x)\left(\log_2\frac{1}{2^{-\ell(x)}} - \log_2\frac{1}{p(x)}\right) = \sum_x p(x)\log_2\frac{p(x)}{K q(x)} = D(p\,\|\,q) + \log_2\frac1K \ge 0.$$
For the converse, take $\ell(x) = \lceil\log_2(1/p(x))\rceil$. Then $2^{-\ell(x)} \le p(x)$, so Kraft's inequality holds and a prefix code with these lengths exists; and $\ell(x) < \log_2(1/p(x)) + 1$, so averaging gives $E[\ell(X)] < H(X) + 1$.

blocks.title: Long messages and physics
blocks.body:
Coding long blocks of independent outcomes together removes the extra $+1$: $n$ independent copies have entropy $nH$, so the best code spends between $nH$ and $nH + 1$ bits per block, that is, $H + 1/n$ bits per symbol. Entropy is exactly the number of bits per symbol needed in the long run.

The physical story is parallel. Boltzmann's entropy of a system with $W$ equally likely microscopic states is $S = k_B\ln W$, which is $k_B$ times the Shannon entropy in nats of the uniform distribution on those states. When the states are not equally likely, Gibbs' formula $S = -k_B\sum p_i\ln p_i$ is Shannon's formula with a different unit. The principle of maximum entropy says that, among all distributions satisfying given constraints, one should choose the one of largest entropy; with a constraint on the mean energy this produces the Boltzmann distribution $p_i \propto e^{-\beta E_i}$.

Find an optimal prefix code for $X$ with probabilities $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18$, and then for $Y$ with probabilities $0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1$. Compare each expected length with the entropy.
blocks.solution:
For $X$, the codewords $0, 10, 110, 111$ have lengths $\log_2(1/p)$ exactly, so
$$E[\ell] = \tfrac12\cdot1 + \tfrac14\cdot2 + \tfrac18\cdot3 + \tfrac18\cdot3 = 1.75 = H(X).$$
The lower bound is achieved, as it must be when every probability is a power of $\tfrac12$.

For $Y$, Huffman's algorithm repeatedly merges the two least likely items: $0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3$, then $0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6$, then $0.6 + 0.4 = 1$. Reading off the depths gives lengths $1, 2, 3, 3$ (for example codewords $0, 10, 110, 111$), with
$$E[\ell] = 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.6 + 0.3 = 1.9,$$
while $H(Y) \approx 1.846$. Huffman codes are known to be optimal among prefix codes, so no code does better than $1.9$ bits per symbol here; the entropy is reached only in the limit of long blocks.

blocks.body: Show that any method that sorts $n$ distinct numbers using comparisons needs, on average over the $n!$ equally likely input orders, at least $\log_2 n!$ comparisons. How many does this give for $n = 5$?
blocks.solution:
Run the algorithm and record the outcome of each comparison as a bit. Different input orders must produce different records, since the algorithm must rearrange them differently, and no record is a proper prefix of another: the algorithm's next step depends only on the outcomes seen so far, so if it stopped on one input after a given record, it would stop at the same moment on any input producing the same outcomes. The records therefore form a prefix code for the uniformly random permutation, whose entropy is $\log_2 n!$. By the source coding theorem the expected number of comparisons is at least $\log_2 n!$.

For $n = 5$, $\log_2 120 \approx 6.907$, so the average is at least $6.907$ and in particular the worst case needs at least $7$ comparisons. Seven do suffice for five numbers; the merge-insertion method of Ford and Johnson achieves this. For large $n$, Stirling's formula gives $\log_2 n! = n\log_2 n - n\log_2 e + O(\log n)$, which is why good sorting algorithms run in about $n\log n$ steps.

blocks.body:
Prove that for $0 < k < n$,
$$\binom{n}{k} \le 2^{n h(k/n)},$$
where $h$ is the binary entropy function, and evaluate both sides for $n = 100$, $k = 25$.
blocks.solution:
Let $p = k/n$. By the binomial theorem,
$$1 = \sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}p^j(1-p)^{n-j} \ge \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.$$
Now $\log_2\left(p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\right) = n\left(p\log_2 p + (1-p)\log_2(1-p)\right) = -n\,h(p)$, so the right-hand side is $\binom nk 2^{-nh(p)}$, and rearranging gives the claim.

For $n = 100$, $k = 25$: $h(1/4) \approx 0.8113$, so the bound is $2^{81.13} \approx 2.64 \times 10^{24}$, while $\binom{100}{25} \approx 2.43 \times 10^{23}$. The bound is off by a factor of about $11$, but on the logarithmic scale it is sharp: since the $j = k$ term is the largest of the $n + 1$ terms, it is at least $1/(n+1)$, giving $\binom nk \ge 2^{nh(k/n)}/(n+1)$. So $\log_2\binom{n}{k} = n\,h(k/n) + O(\log n)$, and entropy is the growth rate of binomial coefficients.

blocks.body:
- The base of the logarithm only sets the unit. Mixing bases inside one calculation is a common source of wrong numbers.
- $H(Y \mid X) \le H(Y)$ holds on average, not for each value: learning a particular $x$ can increase uncertainty. For example, let $X = 0$ with probability $3/4$, in which case $Y = 0$, and $X = 1$ with probability $1/4$, in which case $Y$ is a fair bit. Then $H(Y) = h(1/8) \approx 0.544$, but $H(Y \mid X = 1) = 1$. On average $H(Y \mid X) = 1/4$.
- $D(p\,\|\,q) \ne D(q\,\|\,p)$ in general, and $D$ can be infinite.
- For a density $f$, the differential entropy $-\int f\ln f$ behaves differently: it can be negative (uniform on $[0, 1/2]$ gives $-\ln 2$) and changes under rescaling. Relative entropy between densities keeps all the good properties.

Relative entropy is the exponent in large-deviation estimates: the Chernoff bound from [[moment-generating]] functions for a coin with bias $p$ gives $P(\text{at least } an \text{ heads}) \le 2^{-nD(a\,\|\,p)}$ for $a > p$, with $D$ computed between the coins with biases $a$ and $p$. Maximum likelihood in [[point-estimation]] is the same as minimising relative entropy from the empirical distribution, and the log-likelihood ratio statistics of [[hypothesis-testing]] estimate it. The law of large numbers from [[limit-theorems]] applied to $\log_2(1/p(X_i))$ shows that a long random message of $n$ symbols almost surely has probability $2^{-n(H + o(1))}$, which is the heart of Shannon's theorems. In combinatorics, entropy bounds like the binomial one above are a standard tool alongside the [[probabilistic-method]], and the entropy rate of a [[markov-chains|Markov chain]] measures the information produced per step.

1. Compute the entropy of the total of two fair dice, in bits.
2. Show that if $Y = g(X)$ for some function $g$, then $H(Y) \le H(X)$. (Hint: use the chain rule on $H(X, Y)$ in two ways.)
3. Among distributions on $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ with mean $\mu$, show that the geometric distribution $p(k) = (1-r)r^k$ with $r = \mu/(1 + \mu)$ has the largest entropy, by computing $D(p\,\|\,q) \ge 0$ for $q$ geometric.
4. Twelve coins look alike; one is counterfeit and is either heavier or lighter. Use entropy to show that three weighings on a balance (three outcomes each) cannot be beaten in the worst case.
